newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA SPECTRUM SALE SEEN RAISING A$400 MLN.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA SPECTRUM SALE SEEN RAISING A$400 MLN.

text.p: The planned sale by the Australian government of more mobile telecommunications capacity is unlikely to raise more than A$400 million, brokers Macquarie Equities said in a report.
In July, the government unveiled plans to sell bandwidth in the 800 megahertz (MHz) and 1.8 gigahertz (GHz) band. Some analysts have said the sale could raise A$1 billion.

Macquarie said the frequencies up for grabs would force the winning bidders to introduce new mobile technologies such as DCS 1800 Personal Communications Service (PCS) and TDMA (Time Division Multiple Access) to Australia.
"While DCS 1800 can be closely integrated with the GSM (global systems mobile) networks operated by the existing carriers, the other technologies can't," Macquarie said.

Australia already has one of the highest penetration rates for mobile phones, with one in four people owning a cellular phone. Although the market is still growing, mobile prices are falling and squeezing margins on operators.
"As a consequence, the government's hopes for a U.S.-style billion dollar bonanza from the upcoming mobile communications radio frequency spectrum auctions may be dashed," Macquarie said.

Macquarie said it valued the 1.8 GHz band at about A$250 million. It said the 800 Mhz band was more difficult to estimate because of technology constraints, but it said the spectrum value may be less than A$400 million.
In 1996, the U.S. government raised US$17.9 billion in an auction of similar bands suitable for PCS technology.
The government has restricted existing mobile telephone players Telstra Corp, Optus Communications Pty Ltd and Vodafone Plc from competing in order to promote further domestic competition.
